extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, writers, and general readers interested in artistic philosophy and social criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and ethical guidance for writers/artists: study and meet the needs of your audience (amusement, nourishment, inspiration, beauty) while preserving artistic truth; avoid purely self-indulgent or purely mercenary work and aim to improve public taste and produce lasting work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should serve the world's needs (amusement, food, inspiration, beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist's task is to supply what the World lacks: amusement, food, inspiration, and beauty. (Original phrasing: "It was a Dull World, and needed Amusement. It was a Hungry World, and needed Food. It was a Tired World, and needed Inspiration. It was an Ugly World, and needed Beauty.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret artistic purpose as social: identify the concrete needs of your time/audience (entertainment, intellectual or moral nourishment, spiritual/inspirational uplift, and aesthetic value) and aim to supply them through your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid purely self-expressive art that ignores the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Art made solely for the artist's self-expression will perish with the artist; the first Artist gave only what pleased himself and said, 'When I am dead it will find my work amusing!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: writing that prioritizes private gratification or arcane self-expression at the expense of intelligibility or relevance to readers is unlikely to be received or endure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering solely to low tastes for market success
rubrics_metrics.description: The Merchant-Artist catered to cheap pleasures and prejudices, gave what the World 'liked' and was paid for it, but his work nevertheless died with him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: purely commercializing your art by 'tickling' the audience's lowest or easiest appetites may bring short-term reward but sacrifices longevity and artistic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the audience and meet their needs intelligently
rubrics_metrics.description: The successful Artist 'earnestly studied the needs of the World' and, by intelligence and art, learned and met them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical step: research and empathize with your readership—what are their limits, hungers, and capacities—and craft work that addresses those needs without abandoning artistic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance accessibility with artistic truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Give amusement that is within reach yet genuinely amusing; give inspiration that strikes the heart yet is drawn from eternal truth; give beauty as simple and true. (Original phrasing: 'He gave it Amusement which was within reach of the tastes of that Neglected Child, yet which was in truth Amusing; ... Inspiration which struck to the heart, yet was drawn from Eternal Truth; Beauty as simple as the common flowers the whole world loves, and as true as the stars in heaven.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for work that is approachable but not trivial, emotionally resonant yet grounded in authentic insight, and aesthetically clear yet profound—a synthesis of form and truth that invites and elevates readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek to raise and improve the audience's taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The Artist's work should not simply satisfy present low tastes but should 'improve continually under the influence of his Art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View readership as capable of development: design work that can both please now and expand readers' sensibilities over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure success by service to the world and longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: True success is that 'the World lived, and the Artist lived, and his work lived forever'—art that serves the world endures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize durable cultural impact and usefulness over fleeting applause; durability follows from genuinely serving communal needs while retaining artistic integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: When arguing social or political points, assess advantage not popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: In debates (example: political equality of women) the decisive issue is whether the change is to the advantage of the group and the state, not whether the majority currently requests it ('The point to be decided is whether political equality is to the advantage of women and of the state--not whether either, as a body, is asking for it.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical standard: evaluate policies and ethical positions by their substantive effects and justice, rather than by whether they are presently demanded or popular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test social-theory claims by tracing underlying power structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept asserted 'natural' spheres (e.g., 'society is women's domain') without examining who actually controls social, political, and economic conditions ('Whatever the conditions of the age or place... these conditions are in the hands of men; and these conditions dictate the "society" of that age or place.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical method: analyze historical and structural sources of a social claim; don't conflate accustomed roles with innate capacity or rightful domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake lack of current practice for innate incapacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Abilities often develop with use; exclusionary confinement produces the appearance of incapacity ('Most women spend their whole lives... in the persistent and exclusive contemplation of their own family affairs... If men as a class had been exclusively confined to the occupation of house-service... they would be similarly unlikely to manifest an acute political intelligence.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argumentative caution: when evaluating a group's competence, account for the effects of limited opportunity and training rather than attributing limitations to inherent inferiority.
